title: Remote connections and file transfer
lead: Use SSH for encrypted access to remote Linux systems, SCP for file copies, and rsync for repeatable synchronization. Verify host keys and protect your private key before connecting.
objectives: Use the SSH client with the correct user, host, and port.
Explain the different purposes of host keys and user keys.
Distinguish one-off copies with `scp` from synchronization with `rsync`.
Protect private keys and never blindly accept an unknown host key.

sections.title: A secure session with SSH
body: `ssh user@host` opens an interactive shell on a remote machine. The default port is 22; use `-p` for a different port. `ssh -G host` displays the effective client configuration without connecting.

On first connection, verify the server's host-key fingerprint. Compare it with the fingerprint provided by the server administrator through a trusted channel; do not accept a key just because a prompt appears. A saved host record helps detect identity changes on later connections.

commands.what: Opens an encrypted terminal session on a remote machine.
commands.why: Runs remote commands securely over the network.

commands.what: Connects SSH to the specified TCP port.
commands.where: When the server uses a non-default SSH port.
commands.why: Directs the client to the correct service.

commands.what: Prints effective SSH client settings without connecting.
commands.why: Shows the resolved host, user, and port.

sections.tip: Do not dismiss a host-key-changed warning. If a server was reinstalled, verify its fingerprint through an authorized channel.

sections.title: Key pairs and access security
body: An SSH key consists of a private and a public key. Keep the private key in your own account, never share it, and protect it with suitable file permissions. Add the public key to the target account. A key does not magically eliminate passwords: a passphrase protects the private key.

`ssh-keygen` creates a key pair. `ssh-copy-id` adds the public key to a remote account; use it only for accounts and servers you are authorized to access. Changing server authentication can lock out access.

commands.what: Generates an Ed25519 public/private key pair.
commands.where: In your own account when preparing key-based login.
commands.why: Allows key-based authentication instead of repeated password entry.

commands.what: Displays the fingerprint of a public key.
commands.where: When comparing a key with a trusted reference.
commands.why: Provides a short, comparable identity for the public key.

commands.what: Adds a public key to the remote user's authorized-key list.
commands.where: Only for your own account and an authorized server.
commands.why: Enables key authentication on later connections.

sections.warn: Never send the private-key file (`id_ed25519`) to anyone. Only the `.pub` file may be shared; get permission from the server and account owner.

sections.title: Copy with SCP, synchronize with rsync
body: `scp` copies a file or directory over SSH to or from a remote host. The source/destination form is `user@host:/path`; directories require `-r`. Check in advance whether a destination file will be overwritten.

`rsync` can transfer only changed parts, preserve file attributes, and be run repeatedly. The trailing `/` matters: copying the contents of a source directory to a destination differs from copying the directory itself. Preview the plan with `--dry-run`; `--delete` can remove extra destination files.

commands.where: When sending or retrieving a small number of files.
commands.why: Provides a simple encrypted transfer command.

commands.what: Copies a directory and its contents recursively.
commands.where: When sending a directory to a remote system.
commands.why: Transfers a directory tree in one command.

commands.what: Transfers files in archive mode, synchronizes changes, and shows progress.
commands.where: For repeated backups and directory synchronization.
commands.why: Avoids copying every file on every run.

commands.what: Also deletes destination files that do not exist in the source.
commands.where: Only when the destination must exactly match the source.
commands.why: Removes stale target files; data is lost if the target is wrong.

sections.danger: `rsync --delete` and a misdirected `scp`/`rsync` command can delete or overwrite destination files. Check the target, make a backup, and use `--dry-run`.

t01.text: List the sample transfer files in the simulator with `ls ~/transfer`.

t02.text: List the sample SSH files in the simulator with `ls ~/.ssh`.
t02.hint: This virtual directory contains only a sample configuration and host-key record.

t03.text: Read the sample manifest with `cat ~/transfer/manifest.txt`. Which file is being transferred?
t03.hint: Find the `report.txt` entry in the manifest.

t04.text: Model a one-file transfer: copy `report.txt` as `report.remote.txt`.

t05.text: Predict: which key type does the sample host record use? Check with `grep linux-lab ~/.ssh/known_hosts.sample`.

t06.text: Remove the old local copy `~/transfer/old_copy.txt`, not the source file.
t06.hint: Give `rm` only the exact path of the old copy.

t07.text: Mini project: copy the sample SSH configuration to `~/ops/connection-plan.txt` and verify the `Host linux-lab` and `Port 22` lines.
t07.hint: First run `cp ~/ops/ssh-config.sample ~/ops/connection-plan.txt`, then read it with `cat`.

t08.text: Challenge: prepare a synchronized copy of the report at `~/transfer/sync-copy.txt`.
t08.hint: Copy it with `cp`, then verify its contents with `cat`.

t09.text: Ticket: "One file needs to be copied now; a directory backup needs regular synchronization." Recommend `scp` for the file and `rsync` for synchronization in the support note.
t09.hint: Write both tool names to a note file.

vm.intro: These commands display the client version and configuration. They do not connect to a remote host or transfer files; use only authorized servers for real connections.

v01.title: SSH client version
v01.text: Verify that the SSH client is installed; do not start a connection to a remote system.
differs: The version number varies by distribution; seeing `OpenSSH` is enough.
The output is often written to stderr, but it is visible in the terminal.

v02.title: Effective SSH settings
v02.text: Display the resolved host, user, and port values for `localhost` without opening a connection.
differs: Your user name may not be `student`; that is normal.
Settings in `~/.ssh/config` can affect the output.

v03.title: rsync version
v03.text: Display the rsync version and feature summary; this command does not start a transfer.
differs: The version varies by distribution. If the command is missing, rsync may not be installed.
Follow administrator policy for installation; installing a package is not required for this exercise.

q1.q: Which tool opens a remote Linux shell?
q1.explain: `ssh` opens an encrypted interactive remote session.

q2.q: Which item must remain secret and must not be shared?
q2.explain: The private key stays with its owner; the public key can be added to the target account.

q3.q: Which option previews an rsync operation without making changes?
q3.explain: `--dry-run` shows the planned transfer without making changes.

q4.q: Which tool is better suited to repeated, changing file transfers and synchronization?
q4.explain: `rsync` is designed for incremental, repeatable synchronization.

summary: SSH opens an encrypted terminal session; inspect settings without connecting using `ssh -G`.
Protect the private key and verify the host-key fingerprint through a trusted source.
Use `scp` for straightforward copies and `rsync` for repeated synchronization.
Check direction and target; always use `--dry-run` and a backup before `rsync --delete`.

glossary.meaning: An encrypted network protocol for remote shells and transfers.
A key the server uses to prove its identity to the client.
The shareable part of a key pair added to the remote account.
The secret part of a key pair that must remain protected by its owner.
A preview of planned changes without applying them.
